definition: Tasks where an AI receives human language as input.
Text in, a shorter summary out.
The task of extracting knowledge from documents (for example, companies and the years they were founded).
Given text, return which language it is in.
Text in one language in, the translation in another out.
Find the names of entities in text, such as companies or places.
Audio of speech in, the same words as text out.
Assign text to a type (spam vs. inbox, positive vs. negative).
Choose the correct meaning of a word with several meanings ("bank" as money vs. riverside).
The structure of a sentence; whether words are arranged grammatically. Can be grammatical and still ambiguous ("I saw the man on the mountain with a telescope").
The meaning of words or sentences. Different structures or words can carry the same meaning, and a grammatical sentence can be meaningless ("Colorless green ideas sleep furiously").
A system of rules for generating sentences in a language.
A formal grammar of rewrite rules where each rule applies regardless of the surrounding words.
A rule such as S → NP VP, read "a sentence can be rewritten as a noun phrase followed by a verb phrase."
An actual word in the grammar (she, saw, the). Nothing rewrites it further.
A symbol that can still be expanded (S, NP, VP).
Sentence.
Noun Phrase, a group of words built around a noun ("she", "the city").
Verb Phrase, a group of words built around a verb ("saw the city").
Prepositional Phrase ("with python").
N: Noun. V: Verb. D: Determiner (the, a, an). P: Preposition (to, on, over). ADJ: Adjective (blue, busy, old).
A diagram showing how words group into phrases and phrases into a sentence.
Working out the tree for a sentence from its words.
A rule whose output contains its own symbol (NP → NP PP), allowing sentences of unlimited length from finitely many rules.
The Natural Language Toolkit, a Python library used to define a grammar and parse sentences against it.
nltk's parser, which remembers partial results and returns every valid tree.
The task of splitting a sequence of characters into pieces (tokens).
Splitting characters into words.
Splitting characters into sentences.
Punctuation stuck to words ("remains,"), apostrophes (o'clock), hyphens (pearl-grey), and periods that can mean "Mr." or the end of a sentence.
A contiguous sequence of n items from a sample of text.
A contiguous sequence of n characters.
A contiguous sequence of n words.
An n-gram of 1 item.
An n-gram of 2 items.
An n-gram of 3 items.

A model where each item depends only on a finite number of previous items. For text, it predicts the next word from the last n−1 words, so it can generate text that is locally fluent but lacks meaning and purpose.
The future depends only on the current state, not on how you got there.
A model that represents text as an unordered collection of words, ignoring order and grammar.
Classifying text as positive or negative (for example, product reviews).
P(b | a) = P(a | b) · P(b) / P(a).
A classifier that scores each class as P(class) · P(word₁ | class) · P(word₂ | class) · ..., then normalizes. "Naive" because it assumes words are independent of each other given the class.
How likely a class is before seeing any words, for example P(positive) = positive samples / total samples.
Equal up to a scaling factor. Naive Bayes drops the denominator P(words) and normalizes at the end so the probabilities sum to 1.
Dividing each score by the total so the results sum to 1 (in the slides, 0.6837 and 0.3163).
Adding a value α to each value in the distribution so that no probability is exactly 0.
Additive smoothing with α = 1, pretending each value was seen one more time than it actually was.
The task of finding relevant documents in response to a user query.
Models for discovering the topics of a set of documents.
The number of times a term appears in a document.
Words with little meaning on their own, used to connect other words grammatically (am, by, do, is, which, with, yet).
Words that carry meaning independently (algorithm, category, computer).
A measure of how common or rare a word is across documents: log(total documents / number of documents containing the word). A word in every document scores 0.
A ranking of which words are important in a document, found by multiplying TF by IDF.
A pattern with blanks, such as "When {company} was founded in {year}," used to pull out facts.
A dictionary-like database giving words definitions and broader categories, linking semantically similar words.
Representing a word as a vector with a single 1 and all other values 0. Huge for large vocabularies, and it cannot show that "wrote" and "authored" are similar.
Representing meaning spread across multiple values in a shorter vector. The slides label it "distribution representation." Similar words get similar vectors.
A distributed representation of a single word.

term: "You shall know a word by the company it keeps"
definition: J. R. Firth, 1957. A word's meaning can be inferred from the words around it.
A model for generating word vectors.
A neural network that predicts context words given a target word. Its hidden layer becomes the word vectors.
The word fed in, and the nearby words the network tries to predict.
Relationships show up as vector differences, for example king − man + woman ≈ queen.
A common way to measure how close two vectors are.
